title: Air raid drill in Tashkent and the vastness of the USSR
summary: During the Cuban missile crisis soldiers burst into his hotel room; later trips show the country's size.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, that was in the missile crisis. We were in Tashkent when they had an air raid drill right in the middle of the Cuban missile crisis. And Dave and I were up in our hotel room looking out on the balcony and these soldiers come running up in our room with these Kelishnokov automatic rifles, or something, and scared the Jesus out of me. They drag us into the room, pull the blinds, yell at us in Russian, go through all our drawers and then run back down the street. So we turned out the lights and peeked out and they're sitting up antiaircraft guns out on the square out in front. I thought, "Oh, God, Kennedy's really blown it while we're gone. This is it." That was one of the scariest nights I ever had.
That's quite of a big country, isn't it.
I couldn't really see being so big.

Well, we flew -- the last trip I made in '73, whenever it was, with the George Wein's company with the tribute to Louis Armstrong, we flew from Moscow to Siberia, which is about one-third of the way across the country and which is as far as it was from Moscow to the United States, you know. God, took us something like ten hours to get there.
One city from Moscow, it would be like going from New York to California instead of like New York

Oh, just a short distance up to Leningrad is a five or six hour flight. It's like going to California. Yes, it's an enormous country, all right. I liked both trips there. It was very interesting and I'm glad I went.
